ele-01-ohm.title: Charge, voltage, current and Ohm's Law
ele-01-ohm.theory:
# What electricity is made of

All matter has **electric charges**. The **electron** has a tiny negative charge: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs (C). In a copper wire, billions of electrons are "loose" and can move between atoms. When they all move in the same direction, we have an **electric current**.

## The three quantities you will always use

- **Current (I)**, measured in **amperes (A)**: how much charge passes per second. 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. Formula: `I = Q / t`.
- **Voltage (V)**, measured in **volts (V)**: the "push" that makes charge move. It is the energy each coulomb gains or loses: 1 V = 1 joule per coulomb. A battery cell has 1.5 V; a 9 V battery pushes six times harder.
- **Resistance (R)**, measured in **ohms (Ω)**: how much a material resists the passage of current. Copper has very low resistance; a resistor is a part made to have an exact resistance value.

A useful comparison: think of a water tank. **Voltage** is the height of the water (the pressure), **current** is the flow in the pipe and **resistance** is a thin pipe or a half-closed tap.

# Ohm's Law

Georg Ohm discovered in 1827 that in a resistor the current is proportional to the voltage:

```
V = R × I        I = V / R        R = V / I
```

Example: a 9 V battery across a 1 kΩ (1000 Ω) resistor gives I = 9 / 1000 = 0.009 A = **9 mA** (milliamperes).

## Prefixes that appear all the time

- **k** (kilo) = × 1000 → 4.7 kΩ = 4700 Ω
- **M** (mega) = × 1,000,000
- **m** (milli) = ÷ 1000 → 20 mA = 0.020 A
- **µ** (micro) = ÷ 1,000,000

# How to use the simulator

- The circuit has a **battery (V1)**, an **ammeter (A1)** in series that shows the current, a **resistor (R1)** and a **voltmeter (M1)** in parallel with it.
- The **ground** symbol (the three lines) is the 0 V point: all voltages are measured relative to it.
- **Click** any component or node: the **multimeter** below shows voltage, current and power.
- Components with the value in **green** are adjustable: drag the control or use ◀ ▶ (the values follow the E24 standard series: 1.0 · 1.1 · 1.2 · 1.3 · 1.5 · 1.6 · 1.8 · 2.0 · 2.2 · … · 4.7 · … · 9.1, repeated in each decade: 47 Ω, 470 Ω, 4.7 kΩ…).

ele-02-serie-paralelo.title: Resistors in series and in parallel
ele-02-serie-paralelo.theory:
# Series: only one path

Resistors in **series** sit one after the other: the **same current** flows through all of them, and the source voltage is **divided** among them.

```
Req = R1 + R2 + R3 + …
```

The **voltage divider** is the most famous series circuit: two resistors on a source V. The voltage in the middle is

```
Vout = V × R2 / (R1 + R2)
```

# Parallel: several paths

Resistors in **parallel** connect the same two points: all get the **same voltage**, and the total current is **divided** among the paths. More paths = easier for the current = an equivalent resistance **smaller** than the smallest of them.

```
1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …
Two resistors:  Req = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2)
Two equal:      Req = R / 2
```

## Where this shows up

- The outlets and lamps of a house are in **parallel**: each appliance gets the full 127 V or 220 V and works even if another is off.
- Old Christmas lights were in **series**: one bulb burned out, everything went dark.

# The circuit

The 12 V source feeds **R1 = 100 Ω** in series with the parallel of **R2 = 200 Ω** and **R3** (adjustable). The voltage at node **n2** depends on the value of the parallel R2 ∥ R3. The simulator also computes the **Req** metric: the equivalent resistance the source "sees" (source V ÷ source current).

ele-03-kirchhoff.title: Kirchhoff's Laws and nodal analysis
ele-03-kirchhoff.theory:
# When Ohm's Law alone is not enough

With **two sources** in the circuit, you can't simplify everything into series and parallel. That's where Gustav Kirchhoff's two laws (1845) come in, valid for **any** circuit.

## 1st Law — Current Law (KCL)

A **node** is a point where two or more components connect. Charge doesn't accumulate in a wire, so:

**The sum of the currents entering a node equals the sum of those leaving it.**

```
I_in1 + I_in2 = I_out1 + I_out2
```

This is the **conservation of charge**.

## 2nd Law — Voltage Law (KVL)

Going around any closed path (a **loop**), the sum of the voltages is **zero**: what the sources raise, the resistors drop. This is the **conservation of energy**.

# Nodal analysis: the engineers' method

- Choose a reference node (the **ground**, 0 V).
- Name the voltage of each other node (here only one: **V(n2)**).
- Write the Current Law at each one, replacing each current with (voltage difference) / R.

In our circuit, adding the currents **arriving** at n2 from V1 and V2 and equating them to the one **leaving** through R3:

```
(10 - Vn2)/R1 + (V2 - Vn2)/R2 = Vn2/R3
```

With R1 = R2 = R3 = 1 kΩ, you can solve for Vn2 or, the other way around, find which V2 produces the Vn2 you want. This is exactly how simulators (like this one, and the SPICE used in universities) solve circuits: they build one equation per node and solve the system — **Modified Nodal Analysis**.

ele-04-potencia-energia.title: Power, energy and the electricity bill
ele-04-potencia-energia.theory:
# Power: how fast energy is used

**Power (P)** is energy per time, measured in **watts (W)**. 1 W = 1 joule per second. In an electrical component:

```
P = V × I
```

Combined with Ohm's Law (V = R × I), two other very useful forms appear:

```
P = R × I²        P = V² / R
```

The heat generated in a resistor (the **Joule effect**) is what heats the shower, the iron and the toaster's heating element — and also what melts wires too thin for the current they carry.

# Energy: what the power company charges for

**Energy = Power × Time.** In joules the numbers get huge, so the electricity bill uses the **kilowatt-hour (kWh)**: the energy of 1000 W running for 1 hour.

```
E (kWh) = P (kW) × time (h)
Cost = E (kWh) × rate (R$/kWh)
```

Example: a 100 W TV on 5 h a day for 30 days:

```
E = 0.1 kW × 5 h × 30 = 15 kWh
At a rate of R$ 0.90/kWh → R$ 13.50 per month
```

# Current, wire and circuit breaker

For the same power, **higher voltage = lower current** (I = P / V). That is why a 220 V shower uses thinner wire than a 127 V one of the same power. The **circuit breaker** trips when the current goes above what the wire can handle, before it heats up and catches fire.

## Who uses the most in a house

- Electric shower: 4000 to 7500 W — the champion.
- Air conditioner, electric oven, dryer: 1000 to 3000 W.
- Refrigerator: ~150 W, but on all day.
- LED bulb: 7 to 15 W (an equivalent incandescent used 60 to 100 W).
ele-04-potencia-energia.safety: The household outlet (127 V or 220 V) **kills**. Never open outlets, showers or electrical panels without switching off the breaker and without training — electrical installations are work for a qualified electrician (NR-10 standard). Experiment only with cells, batteries and simulators.

ele-05-thevenin.title: Thévenin, Norton and maximum power transfer
ele-05-thevenin.theory:
# Any circuit becomes a source and a resistor

**Thévenin's Theorem** says that, seen from two terminals, **any** linear circuit (sources and resistors) behaves exactly like:

- a voltage source **Vth** (the open-circuit voltage at the terminals), in series with
- a resistance **Rth** (the resistance seen from the terminals with the sources "turned off": a voltage source becomes a short, a current source becomes an open circuit).

**Norton's Theorem** is its sibling: a current source **In = Vth / Rth** in parallel with the same Rth.

## Computing it for our circuit

The 12 V source feeds a divider (R1 = 6 kΩ, R2 = 3 kΩ) and, after R3 = 1 kΩ, comes the load **RL**.

```
Vth = 12 × 3k / (6k + 3k) = 4 V
Rth = (6k ∥ 3k) + 1k = 2k + 1k = 3 kΩ
```

# Maximum power transfer

The power in the load is

```
P(RL) = Vth² × RL / (Rth + RL)²
```

- RL very small: high current, but almost no voltage across it → little power.
- RL very large: high voltage, but almost no current → little power.
- The maximum happens when **RL = Rth**, and equals **Pmax = Vth² / (4 × Rth)**.

That is why people talk about **impedance matching**: antennas, audio amplifiers and speakers are designed with this idea. But careful: at the maximum power point the load and Rth receive the same power — in the Thévenin equivalent the **efficiency is only 50%**. In the real circuit it can be even worse: here, with RL = 3 kΩ, the 12 V source delivers about 18.7 mW for the load to receive 1.33 mW (≈ 7%), because R1 and R2 also burn energy. The power grid does the opposite (RL much larger than Rth) to avoid wasting energy.

ele-06-rc.title: Capacitors, inductors and the RC transient
ele-06-rc.theory:
# The capacitor stores charge

A **capacitor** is two conducting plates separated by an insulator. Connected to a source, it accumulates charge: **Q = C × V**. The **capacitance C** is measured in **farads (F)** — in practice, in µF, nF and pF. The stored energy is `E = C × V² / 2`.

The current in a capacitor exists only while the voltage **changes**: `i = C × dV/dt`. In direct current, once charged, it is an **open circuit**.

# The inductor stores energy in the magnetic field

An **inductor** is a coil of wire. It opposes changes in **current**: `v = L × di/dt`. The **inductance L** is measured in **henrys (H)**. In direct current, once settled, it is a **wire**. The stored energy is `E = L × I² / 2`.

# The RC transient

When we connect a source V to a resistor R in series with an uncharged capacitor C, the capacitor voltage rises like this:

```
vC(t) = V × (1 − e^(−t/τ))        τ = R × C
```

- **τ (tau)** is the **time constant**, in seconds (Ω × F = s).
- After **1 τ**, the capacitor reaches **63.2%** of the final voltage.
- After **5 τ**, 99.3%: in practice, charged.
- The current does the opposite: it starts at V/R and falls to zero.

In the **RL** circuit, the same curve appears in the current, with **τ = L / R**.

## Where this is used

Timers (the 555 circuit), filters that clean up noise, button *debounce*, the camera flash and the car turn-signal delay are all "one R and one C".

# The oscilloscope

In this lab the simulator runs time: click **▶ Simulate** and the oscilloscope draws the capacitor voltage **V(n2)** (green, left scale) and the current **I(C1)** (yellow, right scale). The simulator measures **τ** by itself: the moment when V(n2) passes 63.2% of the change. If the curve hasn't settled by the end of the simulation (large τ), it estimates τ from the shape of the exponential.

ele-07-fasores.title: Alternating current: phasors, impedance and resonance
ele-07-fasores.theory:
# Alternating current (AC)

At the outlet, the voltage is not constant: it oscillates like a **sine wave**, 60 times per second in Brazil (**60 Hz**).

```
v(t) = Vpeak × sin(2π f t)        ω = 2π f (rad/s)
```

The value shown on appliances (127 V, 220 V) is the **effective value (RMS)**: the DC value that would give the same heating. For sine waves, `Vpeak = Vrms × √2` (the "127 V" reaches peaks of 180 V).

# Phasors: sine waves become arrows

In AC, all the voltages and currents in a circuit have the **same frequency**; what changes is the **amplitude** and the **phase** (the delay). A **phasor** keeps only that: a complex number with magnitude (effective value) and angle. We write `220∠0°` or `10∠−90°`. This way, derivatives become multiplications and the circuit is solved with algebra, as in DC.

# Impedance: the "resistance" in AC

The **impedance Z** (in ohms) is a complex number: `V = Z × I`.

- Resistor: **Z = R** (voltage and current in phase).
- Inductor: **Z = j × XL**, with `XL = ω L = 2π f L` (the current **lags** by 90°).
- Capacitor: **Z = −j × XC**, with `XC = 1 / (ω C)` (the current **leads** by 90°).

In a **series RLC** circuit: `Z = R + j(XL − XC)`, `|Z| = √(R² + (XL − XC)²)` and the **phase angle** is `φ = arctan((XL − XC) / R)`.

# Resonance

XL grows with frequency and XC decreases. At the frequency where **XL = XC** they cancel: the impedance is **minimum (only R)**, the current is **maximum** and the phase is **zero**.

```
f0 = 1 / (2π √(L C))
```

This is how a radio tunes a station: an LC circuit resonates only at its frequency.

# In this lab

The graph shows the **source current as a function of frequency** (logarithmic scale). The red dashed line is the current frequency of the source. Change the frequency and watch the **phase** metric (impedance angle): negative = capacitive, positive = inductive.

ele-08-fator-potencia.title: AC power and power factor correction
ele-08-fator-potencia.theory:
# Three powers

In AC, with voltage and current out of phase by an angle φ, three powers appear:

- **Active power P** (watts, W): the one that becomes useful work and heat. `P = V × I × cos φ`.
- **Reactive power Q** (volt-ampere reactive, var): energy that goes back and forth between the source and the fields of inductors and capacitors, without being consumed. `Q = V × I × sin φ`.
- **Apparent power S** (volt-ampere, VA): the product `S = V × I`, which sizes wires and transformers. `S² = P² + Q²` (the **power triangle**).

# Power factor

```
PF = P / S = cos φ
```

Motors are **inductive** loads (the current lags): a motor with PF = 0.8 draws 25% more current than needed for the same useful power. That extra current heats cables and transformers. That is why, in Brazil, ANEEL rules set the **reference PF at 0.92**: industries and businesses served at medium or high voltage ("Group A") pay for the excess reactive energy when they fall below it. Residential consumers (low voltage) don't pay this charge.

# Correction with capacitors

A capacitor in parallel with the motor supplies **capacitive** reactive power, which cancels part of the motor's inductive reactive power. The active power **doesn't change** — only the line current decreases.

```
Qc = P × (tan φ_before − tan φ_after)
C = Qc / (2π f × V²)
```

Be careful not to overdo it: too much capacitor makes the circuit **capacitive** (PF drops again, now leading).

# The circuit

The motor is modeled by **Rm = 8 Ω** (the part that does work) in series with **Lm = 16 mH** (the magnetic field), at 220 V and 60 Hz. Ammeter A1 shows the line current and the oscilloscope shows the source voltage and current: watch the phase shift shrink as you increase C1. The **phase** metric is the load angle (positive = inductive).

ele-09-retificador.title: Diodes and the full-wave rectifier
ele-09-retificador.theory:
# The diode: a one-way valve

The **diode** lets current pass in one direction only: from the **anode** (the wide side of the symbol's triangle) to the **cathode** (the bar, where the triangle's tip is). The triangle works like an arrow: it points in the direction the current flows. It is made of silicon with two regions, P and N (the **PN junction**).

- **Forward biased** (anode more positive): it conducts, with an almost fixed drop of **≈ 0.7 V** (silicon). The **LED** is a diode that emits light, with a drop of 1.8 to 3.3 V depending on the color.
- **Reverse biased**: it practically doesn't conduct (up to the breakdown voltage).

In the simulator the diode is modeled as a switch: off below 0.7 V; on above it, as 0.7 V in series with a small resistance.

# Rectifier: from AC to DC

Phones, computers and almost all electronics need **direct current**, but the outlet gives **alternating**. The power supply does:

- **Transformer**: steps 127/220 V down to, for example, 12 V RMS (peak 12 × √2 ≈ 17 V).
- **Bridge rectifier** (4 diodes): in the positive half-cycle D1 and D4 conduct; in the negative, D3 and D2. In both cases the current leaves on the same side: the output is **always positive** (full wave). In each half-cycle the current passes through **two** diodes: we lose ≈ 1.4 V.
- **Filter capacitor**: charges at the peaks and feeds the load between them, leaving the voltage almost smooth. The remaining variation is the **ripple**.

```
Ripple ≈ I_load / (2 × f × C)        (full wave: 2 × 60 = 120 peaks per second)
```

The formula is a slightly **pessimistic** estimate: it assumes the capacitor discharges during the whole half-cycle, but it starts charging a little before the peak. The real ripple (the simulator's) is usually 10 to 20% smaller — designing by the formula leaves some margin.

- **Regulator** (for example, the 7805): removes the remaining ripple — a topic for another lesson.

# In this lab

The sine source (17 V peak, 60 Hz) represents the transformer secondary. The oscilloscope shows the source voltage **V(V1)** and the output **V(o1)** across the 100 Ω load. The **ripple** metric is the difference between the maximum and minimum of the output at the end of the simulation; **Vavg** is the average.

ele-10-trifasico.title: Three-phase systems
ele-10-trifasico.theory:
# Why three phases?

Energy is generated and transmitted in **three phases**: three sinusoidal voltages of equal value, shifted by **120°** from each other (A, B and C). Compared to single-phase, three-phase:

- transmits the same power with **less copper** in the cables;
- delivers **constant power** over time (the three waves complement each other) — motors turn smoothly;
- creates a **rotating magnetic field**, which lets the induction motor start by itself.

# Star (Y) connection

The three sources (or loads) have a common point, the **neutral**.

- **Phase voltage** (Vp): between a phase and the neutral.
- **Line voltage** (VL): between two phases. From the phasors, `VL = √3 × Vp`. That is where the **127/220 V** pair comes from (220 = √3 × 127) and the **220/380 V**.
- In star, the line current equals the phase current.

```
Va = 127∠0°   Vb = 127∠−120°   Vc = 127∠120°
Vab = Va − Vb = 220∠30°
```

# Balanced load and neutral current

By the Current Law at the load's star point, the neutral current is the **phasor sum** of the three phase currents:

```
In = Ia + Ib + Ic
```

If the three loads are **equal** (a **balanced** load), the three currents have the same magnitude and are 120° apart: the sum is **zero**. With different loads, current is left over in the neutral, which heats the conductor and unbalances the voltages. That's why electricians spread a building's circuits among the phases.

# Three-phase power

```
P = 3 × Vp × Ip × cos φ = √3 × VL × IL × cos φ
```

# The circuit

Three 127 V sources (60 Hz, 0°, −120°, +120°) feed loads Ra, Rb and Rc connected in star. The star point returns to the source neutral through conductor **Rn** (0.5 Ω), and voltmeter **M1** measures the line voltage between B and C. The oscilloscope shows the three phase voltages.

ele-11-superposicao.title: Superposition, current sources and mesh analysis
ele-11-superposicao.theory:
# Circuits with several sources

Until now almost every circuit had a single source. Real life has several: two batteries in parallel, a solar panel and the grid, a sensor powered by one supply and read by another. There are three classic tools to solve them.

# 1. Superposition

In a **linear** circuit (resistors, capacitors, inductors and sources), the effect of several sources together is the **sum** of the effects of each source alone:

1. Pick one source and "turn off" the others:
   - a **voltage** source turned off = a **short circuit** (0 V across it);
   - a **current** source turned off = an **open circuit** (0 A).
2. Compute the voltage or current you want.
3. Repeat for each source and **add** the results (with their signs!).

⚠ Superposition works for **voltages and currents**, never for **power**: P = R·I² is not linear. Add the currents first and only then compute the power.

# 2. The current source

An ideal **current source** always pushes the **same current**, whatever the voltage across its terminals (the symbol is a circle with an arrow). It appears in the **Norton equivalent** and is a good model for sensors (photodiodes), transistors and battery chargers in their constant-current phase.

# 3. Nodal and mesh analysis

- **Nodal**: one Kirchhoff current law (KCL) equation per node. For node n2 of this lab:

```
(V − 12)/1k + V/2k = I1   →   V = 8 + 666.7 × I1
```

- **Mesh**: a current "circulating" in each window of the circuit and one Kirchhoff voltage law (KVL) equation per mesh. Example: a 10 V source, R1 = 2 Ω only in mesh 1, R2 = 2 Ω only in mesh 2 and R3 = 4 Ω shared:

```
Mesh 1:  10 = (2 + 4)·Ia − 4·Ib
Mesh 2:   0 = −4·Ia + (4 + 2)·Ib
→ Ia = 3 A, Ib = 2 A; R3 carries Ia − Ib = 1 A
```

Circuit simulators (like SPICE and this one) build these equations as a matrix and solve everything at once.

# In the simulator

The 12 V battery feeds node n2 through R1 = 1 kΩ; R2 = 2 kΩ goes to ground; the current source **I1** injects current into the same node. By superposition, V(n2) = **8 V** (effect of the battery) **+ I1 × 666.7 Ω** (effect of I1, with the battery shorted: R1 ∥ R2 = 666.7 Ω).

ele-12-rl.title: Inductors, the RL transient and magnetic energy
ele-12-rl.theory:
# The inductor

An **inductor** is a wire wound in turns (sometimes around an iron core). The current creates a **magnetic field** that stores energy. The property that measures this is the **inductance L**, in **henrys (H)**.

The fundamental rule is **Faraday's/Lenz's law**: the inductor reacts to any **change** in current by producing an opposing voltage:

```
v = L × di/dt
```

That is why the current in an inductor **cannot change suddenly** — it behaves like an electrical "inertia" (just as a capacitor's voltage cannot jump).

# The RL transient

Connecting a source V to a resistor R in series with an inductor L, the current rises exponentially to its final value V/R:

```
i(t) = (V / R) × (1 − e^(−t/τ))        τ = L / R
```

- At **1 τ** the current reaches **63.2%** of its final value; at **3 τ**, 95%; at **5 τ**, 99.3% ("settled").
- The inductor voltage starts at V and falls to zero: at steady DC, an ideal inductor is **a wire**.
- Compare with RC: there τ = R × C; here τ = L / R. **More resistance** makes RC **slower** but RL **faster**.

A real coil has the resistance of its own wire (here **Rb = 50 Ω**), which goes in series in the calculation: τ = L / (R1 + Rb).

# Magnetic energy

```
E = ½ × L × I²
```

When the switch opens, this energy has to go somewhere. Since di/dt becomes huge, v = L·di/dt turns into a **voltage spike**: it makes the spark of a spark plug (hundreds of volts become ~20 kV in the ignition coil) and it **kills transistors** driving relays. The fix is the **flyback diode** in parallel with the coil, which gives the current a path to keep circulating and die out slowly.

# In the simulator

A relay coil has **L = 0.5 H** and **Rb = 50 Ω**, fed from 12 V through the resistor **R1**. The oscilloscope shows the current I(L1) rising and the voltage V(L1) falling.

ele-12-rl.safety: Coils (relays, solenoids, motors, a car's ignition coil) produce **spikes of hundreds or thousands of volts** when their current is suddenly interrupted. Never disconnect an energized coil by hand, and in relay circuits always use a **flyback diode**.

ele-13-led-zener.title: LEDs, the Zener diode and voltage regulators
ele-13-led-zener.theory:
# The real diode

A silicon diode only conducts when the **forward** voltage (anode more positive than cathode) exceeds about **0.6–0.7 V**; below that the current is practically zero. Above it, the current grows **exponentially** (Shockley's equation): a few tenths of a volt more multiply the current by tens. That is why **a diode is never connected straight across a supply**: something must limit the current.

The simulator uses the most common engineering model: an ideal switch with a **knee voltage Vf** and a small **resistance Ron** after it.

# LEDs

An **LED** is a diode that emits light. Its forward voltage depends on the colour (on the semiconductor's band gap):

- red / yellow: **~2 V**;
- green, blue and white: **~3 V**.

The typical current of an indicator LED is **10–20 mA**. The series resistor comes from Ohm's Law applied to the **leftover** voltage:

```
R = (Vsupply − n × Vf) / I        (n LEDs in series)
```

Connecting LEDs **in series** with a single resistor saves energy (the same current lights all of them). Connecting LEDs **in parallel** without a resistor for each one is a bad idea: the one with a slightly lower Vf draws almost all the current, heats up, its Vf drops further… and it burns (**thermal runaway**).

# The Zener diode

Every diode, reverse-biased, breaks down at a high voltage. A **Zener** is made to break down at a **precise, low** voltage (3.3 V, 5.1 V, 12 V…) without damage. In the breakdown region the voltage barely changes with the current: it becomes a **voltage reference**.

## The Zener regulator

```
Vin ── R ──┬── Vout = Vz
           │      │
         Zener   load
```

The resistor must supply the load current **plus** a minimum Zener current (so it keeps regulating):

```
R = (Vin − Vz) / (Iload + Iz,min)
Zener worst case (no load):  Pz = Vz × (Vin − Vz) / R
```

**Integrated regulators** (7805, LM317, LDOs) do the same with an amplifier and a transistor: much more stable, with short-circuit and over-temperature protection. And **switching supplies** (buck, boost) convert voltage at 85–95% efficiency instead of burning the excess as heat.

# In the simulator

Three red LEDs (Vf = 2.0 V and Ron = 10 Ω each) are in series with **R1**, fed from 12 V. The current shows on the multimeter when you click an LED, and the drawing's glow follows the current.

ele-14-filtros.title: RC filters, decibels and the Bode plot
ele-14-filtros.theory:
# Why filter?

Every real signal comes with "dirt": the high-frequency hiss of a microphone, motor noise in a robot's sensor, the mains 60 Hz in a measurement. A **filter** lets the frequencies you care about through and attenuates the others.

# The RC low-pass filter

A resistor in series and a capacitor to ground. At low frequency the capacitor is almost an open circuit (huge XC) and the output copies the input; at high frequency it becomes almost a short and the output drops.

```
Gain   |H| = Vout / Vin = 1 / √(1 + (f / fc)²)
Phase  φ   = −arctan(f / fc)
Cutoff fc  = 1 / (2π R C)
```

At the **cutoff frequency** fc: gain = 1/√2 = **0.707** and phase = **−45°**. Above fc the gain falls **10 times per decade** of frequency.

# Decibels

Since gains range from 1 to 0.0001, engineers use a logarithmic scale, the **decibel**:

```
G(dB) = 20 × log10(Vout / Vin)
```

- gain 1 → 0 dB; 0.707 → **−3 dB**; 0.1 → −20 dB; 0.01 → −40 dB; 10 → +20 dB.
- That is why fc is also called the **−3 dB frequency** (the power halves).
- Above fc the RC low-pass falls **−20 dB per decade** (1st-order filter). Two stages give −40 dB/decade (2nd order).

The plot of gain (in dB) and phase against frequency on a log scale is the **Bode plot**.

# Other filters

- **High-pass**: swap R and C (capacitor in series, resistor to ground). It blocks DC and low frequencies — it is the "coupling capacitor" of audio inputs.
- **Band-pass** and **band-stop**: combine both, or use a resonant LC (next lesson).
- **Active filters** (with operational amplifiers) have gain and high orders without inductors.

Examples: the anti-aliasing filter before an analog-to-digital converter, the crossover that splits bass and treble in a speaker, the RC on a button pin to clean its bounce.

# In the simulator

The plot shows **V(n2)** (the output) against frequency, from 10 Hz to 100 kHz, with 1 V at the input — so V(n2) is already the gain. The dashed line marks 1 kHz, the source frequency. The metric **ph(n2)** is the output phase.

ele-15-ressonancia-paralela.title: Parallel resonance, quality factor and selectivity
ele-15-ressonancia-paralela.theory:
# The tank circuit

In the phasor lesson, the **series** RLC had **minimum** impedance at resonance. Now the inductor and the capacitor are **in parallel** — the so-called **tank circuit**. At the resonant frequency the inductor current (lagging 90°) and the capacitor current (leading 90°) are equal and opposite: they **cancel** on the outside, and the energy keeps "swapping" between them inside.

```
f0 = 1 / (2π √(L C))      (the same formula as the series one)
```

- **Series LC** at resonance: minimum impedance (≈ short) → lets f0 through.
- **Parallel LC** at resonance: **maximum** impedance (ideally infinite) → **blocks** f0.

In a real tank the maximum impedance is finite: the losses (wire and core resistance) show up as a parallel resistor, **Rp**. At resonance the tank is exactly **Rp**.

# Quality factor (Q) and bandwidth

**Q** measures how "sharp" the resonance is: how much energy is stored compared with what is lost per cycle.

```
Parallel:  Q = R / XL = R / (2π f0 L)      (R = resistance in parallel with the tank)
Series:    Q = XL / R
Bandwidth: BW = f0 / Q      (between the −3 dB points)
```

- High Q (50–500): narrow, **selective** resonance — it tunes one station and rejects its neighbours.
- Low Q: a wide, "soft" response.
- Anything in parallel **loads** the tank: here the source sees R1 ∥ Rp = 909 Ω, so the loaded Q is 909 / 67.4 ≈ 13.5 (much lower than the tank's own Q, 10 000 / 67.4 ≈ 148).

# Where it shows up

- Tuning AM/FM radios and NFC (13.56 MHz) — the tank selects one frequency.
- LC **oscillators**: the tank sets the frequency and an amplifier makes up the losses.
- Filters that **reject** one frequency (the tank in series with the line), e.g. harmonics in power systems.

# In the simulator

The 10 V source feeds the tank (**L = 10 mH**, **C = 2.2 µF**, losses **Rp = 10 kΩ**) through **R1 = 1 kΩ**. The plot shows V(n2), the tank voltage, against frequency. Far from resonance the tank "shorts" the signal; near f0 it opens up and the voltage rises to 10 × 10k/11k ≈ 9.09 V.

ele-16-transformador.title: Transformers and electromagnetic induction
ele-16-transformador.theory:
# Induction: the field that makes voltage

In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered that a **changing magnetic field** passing through a coil induces a voltage in it:

```
v = N × dΦ/dt        (N turns, Φ = magnetic flux)
```

The sign (**Lenz's law**) says the induced voltage tries to oppose the change that created it. It is the principle of generators, motors, wireless chargers, metal detectors… and **transformers**.

# The transformer

Two coils wound on the **same iron core**. The alternating current in the **primary** creates a flux that changes 60 (or 50) times a second; that flux passes through the **secondary** and induces a voltage in it. Since the flux is the same, so is the voltage per turn:

```
V1 / V2 = N1 / N2          (turns ratio, a)
I1 / I2 = N2 / N1          (the current does the opposite)
P1 = P2  →  V1·I1 = V2·I2  (ideal transformer)
```

- **Step-down** (N2 < N1): 220 V → 12 V in an old charger, 13.8 kV → 220/127 V on the pole.
- **Step-up** (N2 > N1): at the power plant, from ~13.8 kV to 138, 500 or 765 kV.
- **Isolation** (N1 = N2): same voltage, but the secondary is **isolated** from the grid — safer.

## Why it only works on AC

A **direct** current creates a **constant** flux: dΦ/dt = 0, no voltage is induced. Worse: the primary becomes just the wire's resistance, the current shoots up and the transformer burns.

## Reflected impedance

A load Z on the secondary "appears" on the primary multiplied by a²:

```
Z1 = (N1/N2)² × Z2
```

That is how an output transformer matches an 8 Ω speaker to a valve amplifier of a few kΩ (maximum power transfer!).

# The real transformer

- **Copper losses**: R·I² in the windings (they grow with the load).
- **Iron losses**: **hysteresis** (the iron "resists" reversing its magnetization) and **eddy currents** circulating inside the core — that is why the core is made of **thin insulated sheets** (laminated) of silicon steel.
- Efficiency: 95% (small ones) to over 99% (power transformers).
- The nameplate gives the rating in **VA** or **kVA** (apparent power), not in W.

# Why transmit at high voltage

For the same power, P = V × I: **10 times the voltage = 10 times less current**. The line loss is R × I², so it falls **100 times**. Without transformers (and therefore without AC), every neighbourhood would need its own power plant — that argument made Tesla and Westinghouse's AC beat Edison's DC in the "war of the currents".
ele-16-transformador.safety: The primary of a transformer plugged into the wall is at **127/220 V** (or 230 V), and distribution transformers reach **13.8 kV or more**: they are lethal. A transformer that is switched off may still be energized from the other side (backfeed). Don't open power supplies, chargers or panels; work on installations is for qualified professionals.

ele-17-ampop.title: Operational amplifiers
ele-17-ampop.theory:
# The "building block" of analog electronics

The **operational amplifier** (op-amp) is an integrated circuit with two inputs — **non-inverting (+)** and **inverting (−)** — and one output. It amplifies the **difference** between the inputs with a huge gain (10⁵ to 10⁶):

```
Vout = A × (V+ − V−)        A ≈ 100,000 or more
```

With such a gain, any millivolt of difference drives the output close to the supply (**saturation**). The trick is **negative feedback**: connecting the output back to the inverting input through resistors. Then the circuit depends **only on the resistors**, not on the chip's gain.

# The golden rules (ideal op-amp with negative feedback)

1. **No current** flows into the inputs (infinite input impedance).
2. The output does whatever it takes to make **V+ = V−** (the "virtual short").

With them, every classic circuit comes out in two lines.

# Classic circuits

```
Inverting:          Vout = −(Rf / Rin) × Vin
Non-inverting:      Vout = (1 + Rf / Rg) × Vin
Follower (buffer):  Vout = Vin        (gain 1, isolates a weak source from a load)
Inverting summer:   Vout = −Rf × (V1/R1 + V2/R2 + …)
```

- **Inverting**: the + input goes to ground; by the virtual short the − input also sits at 0 V ("virtual ground"). The current Vin/Rin all flows through Rf (rule 1), so Vout = −Rf·Vin/Rin.
- **Non-inverting**: Vin enters at +; Rf and Rg form a divider of the output that must reproduce Vin at the − input.
- **Summer**: it is the audio mixer and the basis of digital-to-analog converters.
- **Integrator** (a capacitor in place of Rf): the output is the integral of the input — the "I" of an analog PID controller.
- **Comparator** (no feedback): the output goes to its positive or negative maximum depending on whether V+ > V−. With **positive** feedback it becomes a **Schmitt trigger** (hysteresis against noise).

# Limits of the real op-amp

- **Saturation**: the output can't go beyond the supply voltages (a rail-to-rail op-amp gets close to them; a 741 stays ~1.5–2 V below).
- **Gain-bandwidth product (GBW)**: an op-amp with a 1 MHz GBW gives a gain of 10 up to 100 kHz, a gain of 100 only up to 10 kHz.
- **Slew rate**: the output's maximum speed (V/µs). Large, fast signals turn "triangular".
- Offset voltage, bias currents and noise matter in precision instrumentation.

# Gain in decibels

```
G(dB) = 20 × log10(|Vout / Vin|)      gain 10 → 20 dB, 100 → 40 dB, 1000 → 60 dB
```

ele-18-motores.title: Electric motors: DC, induction and drives
ele-18-motores.theory:
# The force that turns the world

About **half of the world's electrical energy** is used by motors. All of them use the same physics: a current-carrying conductor inside a magnetic field feels a force (the **Lorentz force**, F = B·I·L). Arrange several conductors around a shaft and you have **torque**.

```
Mechanical power:  P = T × ω        ω (rad/s) = 2π × n (rpm) / 60
```

# The DC motor

- Magnets (or field coils) on the **stator**; the **rotor** coil gets its current through **brushes and a commutator**, which reverse the current every half turn.
- As it spins, the rotor generates a **back EMF** E = k·ω that opposes the applied voltage: the speed rises until E ≈ V. That is why **speed is almost proportional to voltage** and **torque to current** (T = k·I).
- At start-up E = 0: the current is huge (only the winding resistance limits it).
- Variants: **brushless (BLDC)** — no brushes, commutated by an electronic controller (drones, fans, electric cars); **stepper motor** — turns in exact steps (3D printers); **servo motor** — motor + position sensor + control.

# The three-phase induction motor

Industry's workhorse: simple, rugged, brushless.

- The three phases in the stator create a **rotating magnetic field**, which turns at the **synchronous speed**:

```
ns = 120 × f / p        (f in Hz, p = number of poles)
60 Hz: 2 poles → 3600 rpm; 4 poles → 1800 rpm; 6 poles → 1200 rpm
```

- The field induces currents in the rotor (the "squirrel cage") and these are dragged along by the field. But the rotor never reaches ns — if it did, there would be no induction and no torque. The difference is the **slip**:

```
s = (ns − n) / ns        (typically 2–5% at rated load)
```

- **Reversing the direction**: swap **any two phases**.
- **Starting**: direct-on-line, the current reaches 6–8× the rated value. **Star-delta** starting cuts that current to 1/3; a **soft starter** controls it electronically.

## Nameplate and efficiency

The nameplate gives the **mechanical power at the shaft** (kW or hp), voltage, current, power factor and efficiency. The electrical input power of a three-phase motor is:

```
Pin = √3 × V × I × PF          efficiency η = Pout / Pin
```

# Drives

A **frequency inverter** (VFD) rectifies the mains and "builds" a new AC with a variable frequency (PWM): changing f changes ns, and the induction motor becomes a **variable-speed** motor, keeping V/f constant. It saves a lot of energy in pumps and fans, where power falls with the cube of the speed.
ele-18-motores.safety: Industrial motors are **three-phase (220/380 V or more)** and turn with enough torque to crush hands. Before any maintenance: **switch off, lock out and tag out** (LOTO) the supply and wait for the shaft to stop; frequency inverters keep dangerous voltage in their capacitors for minutes after being switched off. Work on panels and motors is for qualified professionals.

ele-19-condutores.title: Conductor sizing and voltage drop
ele-19-condutores.theory:
# The wire is a resistor too

The cables of an installation have a small but non-zero resistance:

```
R = ρ × L / A
ρ (copper, 20 °C) ≈ 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m      L in metres, A in mm²
```

A circuit has a **go and return** path (phase and neutral, or two phases): the electrical length is **2 × the distance**. Example: 25 m of 2.5 mm² cable → R = 0.0172 × 50 / 2.5 = **0.344 Ω** for the whole loop.

This resistance causes two problems:

- **Voltage drop**: ΔV = R × I. The appliance gets less voltage — the shower heats less, the motor loses torque and runs hot, the lamp flickers.
- **Heating**: P = R × I² turns into heat inside the conduit.

# The two criteria of the wiring code

You choose the **smallest cross-section** that meets **all** criteria (the main ones):

1. **Current-carrying capacity** (ampacity): PVC insulation withstands 70 °C. Typical values for 2 loaded conductors in a conduit embedded in a wall (method B1, NBR 5410 / IEC 60364-5-52):

```
1.5 mm² → 17.5 A    2.5 mm² → 24 A    4 mm² → 32 A
6 mm²   → 41 A      10 mm²  → 57 A
```

2. **Voltage drop**: at most **4%** on final circuits (from the distribution board).

There are also **minimum cross-sections** (1.5 mm² for lighting, 2.5 mm² for sockets) and **coordination with the protection**: the breaker's current must lie between the circuit current and the cable's capacity (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz).

# In the simulator

A **5500 W / 220 V** electric shower (resistance **Rch = 8.8 Ω**, 25 A rated) is **40 m** from the board. The resistor **Rc** stands for the whole cable, go and return (80 m of copper): choose the cross-section and read the current on the ammeter, the voltage reaching the shower on the voltmeter and the heat lost in the cable by clicking Rc. Since the shower is a pure resistance, the AC RMS values can be computed as if it were DC.

ele-19-condutores.safety: Sizing and installing circuits is work for a **qualified electrician or engineer**, following the wiring code (NBR 5410 in Brazil, IEC 60364, the NEC…). A cable that is too thin heats up, melts its insulation and is one of the main causes of **house fires**. Never replace a breaker with a bigger one "because it kept tripping": the breaker protects the cable.

ele-20-protecao.title: Short circuits, protection and earthing
ele-20-protecao.theory:
# Overload and short circuit

- **Overload**: a current somewhat above normal for a long time (too many appliances on a circuit). The cable heats up slowly.
- **Short circuit**: the phase touches the neutral, another phase or an earthed enclosure. The current is limited only by the resistance of the cables and the grid: **hundreds or thousands of amperes** within milliseconds.

# The thermal-magnetic circuit breaker

- **Thermal trip** (bimetallic strip): takes seconds to minutes; it handles **overload**.
- **Magnetic trip** (coil): instantaneous (≈ 10 ms), it handles **short circuits**. It only acts above a multiple of the rated current In, according to the **curve**:

```
Curve B: 3 to 5 × In      (resistive circuits, long cables)
Curve C: 5 to 10 × In     (general use, small motors)
Curve D: 10 to 20 × In    (motors and transformers with large inrush)
```

To **guarantee** an instantaneous trip, the fault current must exceed the **upper limit** of the band (10 × In for curve C).

# A fault to the enclosure and the protective conductor (PE)

If the phase touches the metal enclosure of a washing machine, the enclosure becomes live. In the **TN-S** system (the most common in buildings), the **protective conductor PE** (green/yellow wire) connects the enclosure back to the transformer's neutral. The **fault loop** is formed:

```
Ifault = V / (Rsource + Rphase + Rpe)
Touch voltage on the enclosure:  Vtouch = Ifault × Rpe
```

Two things must happen: the fault current must be **large enough** for the breaker to trip **at once**, and the enclosure voltage meanwhile must stay **low**. The reference conventional touch-voltage limit in dry locations is **50 V** (AC). That is why the codes require the PE to have the **same cross-section as the phase** up to 16 mm²: a thin PE raises Rpe — and with it the touch voltage — and lowers the fault current.

# The RCD (residual-current device)

The RCD compares the current going out on the phase with the one returning on the neutral. If the difference exceeds **30 mA** (someone getting a shock, or leakage to earth), it trips in ~30 ms. **The breaker protects the cable; the RCD protects people.** Codes require RCDs in bathrooms, kitchens, outdoor areas and sockets in wet areas.

## Other elements

- **Equipotential bonding**: connecting all metal parts (pipes, structures) to the same earth bar.
- **SPD** (surge protective device): protects against surges from lightning and switching.
- **TT system**: the PE goes to its own earth electrode; the fault current is small and only the **RCD** guarantees disconnection.

# In the simulator

A fault connects the phase to an appliance's enclosure on 127 V. **Rs = 0.1 Ω** is the grid impedance, **Rf = 0.172 Ω** is the phase conductor (40 m of 4 mm²) and **Rpe** is the protective conductor, which you choose. The ammeter shows the fault current; the voltmeter, the enclosure voltage. The breaker is **20 A, curve C**.

ele-20-protecao.safety: Electric shock **kills**: **30 mA** through the chest can already cause fibrillation. Never touch live boards, sockets or earthing; never "test" an enclosure with your hand. Installations, earthing and protection are designed and built by **qualified professionals** (wiring code and electrical-safety rules), with proper measuring equipment.
